The clerk behind the counter was a thin man with ink-stained fingers and spectacles perched low on his nose. The board's papers had been pinned and re-pinned, corners curling, older sheets bleeding through the newer ones. Four contracts sat at eye level on the Novice strip, each on a standardized slip with the Guild's faint enchantment shimmering in the ink—a small glowing line at the bottom that read ACTIVE.

Most were culling work. Striders, by the look of it—two separate contracts for them, one out at the old quarry track east of the city, another down at the eel-weirs on the Reed Flats, both paying modestly, both noting the same caution in small print: kills counted toward a total, and the creatures ran in groups. A third offered more coin for burrow boars rooting up terraced vineyards on the Duskreach slopes, though the reported size of the beasts sat above his level. The last was the boldest of the lot: the Mossback Warrens, level one, the goblin hill half a day east—Guild-posted, paying the best of the four, with a blunt risk line about groups and stronger foes.

Behind him, the two women at the map table had stopped arguing. One, a stocky woman with a crossbow slung across her back, glanced at the board and then at Alaric with the brief appraisal of someone weighing whether a new face meant competition. She went back to her map.

The clerk's queue had thinned. The bloodied-armed woman was gone; a boy now leaned at the bar arguing the price of a breakfast.

He pulled the Mossback slip from the board and brought it to the counter. The clerk took it, checked the seal, and flipped open the ledger to a fresh line. "Mossback Warrens, level one. Solo?" Mossy on top, palisade stakes stuck in it like a bad haircut. You can't miss it." The crossbow woman at the map table snorted quietly at something, not looking up. "That's the lot," the clerk said, and beckoned the boy at the bar forward. "Next." ACTIVE SCENE — Dammar · SHORT
He left Ashbridge by the east gate with the contract slip folded inside his robe. The cobbles gave way to packed mud, the mud to a rutted track running between hedgerows still dripping from the morning's rain. Cart ruts cut deep and doubled, filled with water that threw the grey sky back up at him. The city fell behind. Fields took over—turnip strips, a pasture with three listless sheep—then a stretch of common scrub where the track widened and the wheel ruts hardened into old quarry stone. He passed the quarry itself an hour or so out: a grey scar in the hillside, terraced and flooded at the bottom, a rusted windlass leaning over nothing. A painted board nailed to a post, older than him, read DUSKREACH MINING CONCERN — NO BLASTING WITHOUT LEAVE, the letters half flaked away. Past the quarry the track narrowed. Gorse crowded both sides. Somewhere off to his left a woodpecker hammered and stopped, hammered and stopped. Twice he crossed boot prints in the soft ground—once a single set, human-sized, going the way he was going and looking a few days old; once something else, a splayed three-toed print pressed deep at the track's edge, hours old at most. He gave both a look and walked on. The moss-grown hill showed itself early in the afternoon, exactly as promised: a green rounded hump off the track's north side, old palisade stakes jutting from its crown at crooked angles, some fallen, a few charred. A dark opening showed halfway up the slope, and smoke—thin, greasy, standing straight in the still air—rose from somewhere behind the hill's shoulder. He was still a hundred paces down the track, weighing the ground between gorse and hillside, when a voice came from his right. "Oi. You walking to that hill?" A man sat back in the gorse off the track's edge where he'd clearly been resting—a scrawny fellow in a patched fisherman's oilskin, a hand-line wound on a bottle and a creel of reeds at his feet, a scattering of pale roots dug up beside him. Forty-something, unshaven, one eye narrowed against the light. He didn't get up. "Because if you're going to the Warrens, there's things worth knowing first. And knowing's not free, see." He picked up one of the roots and turned it in his fingers. "Not coin, neither. You've a look of the Guild about you. I want a word put in for me, up at the hall, when you come back alive. Dammar's my name. They know me there."

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
He left Ashbridge by the east gate with the contract slip folded inside his robe. The cobbles gave way to packed mud, the mud to a rutted track running between hedgerows still dripping from the morning's rain. Cart ruts cut deep and doubled, filled with water that threw the grey sky back up at him.

The city fell behind. Fields took over—turnip strips, a pasture with three listless sheep—then a stretch of common scrub where the track widened and the wheel ruts hardened into old quarry stone. He passed the quarry itself an hour or so out: a grey scar in the hillside, terraced and flooded at the bottom, a rusted windlass leaning over nothing. A painted board nailed to a post, older than him, read DUSKREACH MINING CONCERN — NO BLASTING WITHOUT LEAVE, the letters half flaked away.

Past the quarry the track narrowed. Gorse crowded both sides. Somewhere off to his left a woodpecker hammered and stopped, hammered and stopped. Twice he crossed boot prints in the soft ground—once a single set, human-sized, going the way he was going and looking a few days old; once something else, a splayed three-toed print pressed deep at the track's edge, hours old at most. He gave both a look and walked on.

The moss-grown hill showed itself early in the afternoon, exactly as promised: a green rounded hump off the track's north side, old palisade stakes jutting from its crown at crooked angles, some fallen, a few charred. A dark opening showed halfway up the slope, and smoke—thin, greasy, standing straight in the still air—rose from somewhere behind the hill's shoulder.

He was still a hundred paces down the track, weighing the ground between gorse and hillside, when a voice came from his right.

"Oi. You walking to that hill?"

A man sat back in the gorse off the track's edge where he'd clearly been resting—a scrawny fellow in a patched fisherman's oilskin, a hand-line wound on a bottle and a creel of reeds at his feet, a scattering of pale roots dug up beside him. Forty-something, unshaven, one eye narrowed against the light. He didn't get up.

"Because if you're going to the Warrens, there's things worth knowing first. And knowing's not free, see." He picked up one of the roots and turned it in his fingers. "Not coin, neither. You've a look of the Guild about you. I want a word put in for me, up at the hall, when you come back alive. Dammar's my name. They know me there."

The word was barely out of him before heat gathered along the staff's length and a lance of fire tore across the track. It took the strider full in the breast. Feathers of flame ran up its neck; the hooked beak snapped once at nothing, and the whole stilt-legged frame went over sideways, legs folding wrong, one kicking a slow groove in the mud before it lay still. The smell of scorched hide drifted across the track. Smoke curled off the pale body. Dammar's head rose slowly out of the gorse, both eyes wide now. "Well." He got to his feet, keeping a cautious eye on the dead bird even so. "Well, that's one way. Quicker than my way, certainly." He came back to the track's edge but wouldn't pass close to the carcass, giving it a wide, respectful berth. "Two fingers, I told you. It's good to see one go the other round." He looked Alaric up and down again, reassessing, and something in his manner shifted—the casualness gone, replaced by the careful friendliness of a man recalculating who he's talking to. "Contract work, is it? The Warrens?" He didn't wait for an answer to that; his eyes had already gone to the hill. "Then take what I said for worth. And—" he hesitated, scratching under his oilskin collar, "—the boy, mind. If you happen on him. I'd not forgotten." A faint warmth stirred against Alaric's ribs where the small pouch hung; the strider's take—two long feathers and a pair of curved talons, sharp as knives—had settled into it without his ever bending over the carcass. Something similar ran through him, deeper than warmth: a settling, a quiet click of things sliding into place, and five points of unspent strength waiting at his fingertips for wherever he chose to put them. Dammar hoisted his creel onto his shoulder. "I'll be off to the quarry while the light holds. Unless—" he nodded at the hill, then back at Alaric, plainly curious and plainly deciding how much curiosity was safe, "—unless you'd rather I stopped here a while. In case. The word was barely out of him before heat gathered along the staff's length and a lance of fire tore across the track. It took the strider full in the breast. Feathers of flame ran up its neck; the hooked beak snapped once at nothing, and the whole stilt-legged frame went over sideways, legs folding wrong, one kicking a slow groove in the mud before it lay still. The smell of scorched hide drifted across the track. Smoke curled off the pale body.

Dammar's head rose slowly out of the gorse, both eyes wide now.

"Well." He got to his feet, keeping a cautious eye on the dead bird even so. "Well, that's one way. Quicker than my way, certainly." He came back to the track's edge but wouldn't pass close to the carcass, giving it a wide, respectful berth. "Two fingers, I told you. It's good to see one go the other round."

He looked Alaric up and down again, reassessing, and something in his manner shifted—the casualness gone, replaced by the careful friendliness of a man recalculating who he's talking to.

"Contract work, is it? The Warrens?" He didn't wait for an answer to that; his eyes had already gone to the hill. "Then take what I said for worth. And—" he hesitated, scratching under his oilskin collar, "—the boy, mind. If you happen on him. I'd not forgotten."

A faint warmth stirred against Alaric's ribs where the small pouch hung; the strider's take—two long feathers and a pair of curved talons, sharp as knives—had settled into it without his ever bending over the carcass. Something similar ran through him, deeper than warmth: a settling, a quiet click of things sliding into place, and five points of unspent strength waiting at his fingertips for wherever he chose to put them.

Dammar hoisted his creel onto his shoulder.

"I'll be off to the quarry while the light holds. Unless—" he nodded at the hill, then back at Alaric, plainly curious and plainly deciding how much curiosity was safe, "—unless you'd rather I stopped here a while. In case. A man on the track's worth something if you come out of that place running."

What had looked like a green hump resolved into a proper ruin: old quarry terraces cut into the near side, moss eating the stone, and along the crown a broken line of blackened stakes—the rotted skull of a palisade somebody had raised there a lifetime ago. The ground helped him: a shallow fold ran along the hill's flank like an old scar, deep enough to hide a crouched man, floored with fern and soft moss that took his steps without a sound. The wind lay against his face, coming off the hill, carrying the smell of wet stone and, faintly now, woodsmoke and something sourer underneath—rot, or offal. He followed the fold upward until it shallowed out against a tumbled slab, and there he stopped, fern brushing his chin, and looked up. Its back was to the east fold. Below it, the burnt doorway of the ruin gaped at the hill's foot on the far side, out of this sightline. name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
Dammar touched two fingers to his brow—not quite a salute, but near kin to one—and trudged off west with his creel, giving the dead strider its wide berth. His footsteps faded down the track.

The hill grew as Alaric walked. What had looked like a green hump resolved into a proper ruin: old quarry terraces cut into the near side, moss eating the stone, and along the crown a broken line of blackened stakes—the rotted skull of a palisade somebody had raised there a lifetime ago. Smoke rose from behind the far shoulder, thin and greasy, bending south on the wind. Nearer, the hill's foot was quiet. A crow worked at something in the grass. Somewhere a woodpecker knocked and stopped.

At the edge of the old quarry workings Alaric left the track and bent low, keeping to the shadow of a cut bank, then swung east as Dammar had said. The ground helped him: a shallow fold ran along the hill's flank like an old scar, deep enough to hide a crouched man, floored with fern and soft moss that took his steps without a sound. The wind lay against his face, coming off the hill, carrying the smell of wet stone and, faintly now, woodsmoke and something sourer underneath—rot, or offal.

He followed the fold upward until it shallowed out against a tumbled slab, and there he stopped, fern brushing his chin, and looked up.

The palisade's crown was fifty paces above him and clear across its length. Four stakes still stood at that end of the hill, and the second from the left, as Dammar had counted it, had a shape on it—a small hunched figure, green-grey, cross-legged on the flattened top of the stake like a scarecrow that had learned to sit. Still. Too still for a living thing at first glance, until it shifted, scratched itself, and turned its head slowly toward the west track, the way any walker would come. Its back was to the east fold. Below it, the burnt doorway of the ruin gaped at the hill's foot on the far side, out of this sightline.

Between Alaric and the summit, the fold kept on, and the slope steepened into loose scree that would talk underfoot.

The lookout sat where it sat, staring west, unaware.
